title: 1 Peter
subtitle: Strangers in the world, at home in God's house
lead: 1 Peter is a letter to scattered churches in what is now Turkey, traditionally from the apostle Peter, sent from 'Babylon', most likely Rome. Whether Peter wrote it himself, wrote it through his helper Silvanus, or whether his followers wrote it in his name after his death is debated (see Authorship). Its readers were probably mostly Gentile converts who had left their families' gods and their neighbors' feasts, though ancient readers such as Eusebius, and later Calvin, took them to be Jewish believers of the Dispersion. They were slandered and insulted for their faith, and slaves among them could be beaten. The letter calls them 'temporary residents' and 'resident aliens': people who no longer fit where they live, because their home is with God.

Its answer to suffering is hope. God has given them new birth into a living hope through Christ's resurrection (1:3). They are living stones built into God's house, 'a chosen family, a royal priesthood, a holy nation' (2:9). They are to do good, return blessing for abuse, honor the emperor but fear God alone, and follow Christ, who suffered unjustly and left them 'a model to trace' (2:21). The letter also holds two of the most debated verses in the New Testament: Christ's proclamation 'to the spirits in prison' (3:19) and the baptism that 'saves you now as well' (3:21).
facts: Traditionally Peter, the apostle (1:1), writing 'through Silvanus' (5:12). Many scholars, perhaps most today, hold that it was written in Peter's name by his followers in Rome. See the authorship table.
If Peter wrote it, before his death in Rome, in the 60s AD. If a Petrine circle wrote it, the proposals run from about AD 70 to the reign of Trajan (about AD 112).
'Babylon' (5:13), which early tradition and most scholars take to be Rome.

Believers in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, five regions of Asia Minor: probably mostly Gentile converts, though some have held they were Jewish believers or mixed churches (see Who it was for).
A circular letter: greeting, blessing, teaching on holiness and identity, a household code, teaching on suffering, words to elders, greetings.
Greek, polished, with many quotations from the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament.
authorship: It opens 'From Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ' (1:1), calls the writer 'a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ' (5:1), and says he wrote 'through Silvanus' and sends greetings from Mark (5:12-13).

Polycarp's Letter to the Philippians (early 100s) echoes it many times (for example 1:8 in chapter 1 and 2:22, 24 in chapter 8). Eusebius reports that Papias used 'testimonies ... from that of Peter' and lists 1 Peter among the books acknowledged by all, while 2 Peter was disputed (Church History 3.3; 3.25; 3.39).

Peter wrote it, perhaps with a helper, from Rome before his death in the 60s. Its supporters point to the letter's own claim (1:1; 5:1); its likenesses to Peter's speeches in Acts; echoes of Jesus' sayings that suggest an eyewitness (compare 1:13 with Luke 12:35, 2:12 with Matthew 5:16, and 3:14 with Matthew 5:10); its early and wide acceptance (see Early use; 2 Peter 3:1 also refers to an earlier letter of Peter); and the point that a writer borrowing a name for a letter this close to Paul's would more likely have used Paul's. Karen Jobes leans toward Peter: 'the simplest explanation might be the likeliest: that the apostle Peter is the author, with amanuensis assistance a possible but not necessary explanatory factor'.

The 'secretarial hypothesis' holds that Peter dictated or approved the letter and Silvanus (5:12), a leader of the Jerusalem church who had traveled with Paul (Acts 15:22, 40; 1 Thessalonians 1:1), gave it its Greek form. That would answer the main objection, the polished Greek, and would explain the likeness to Paul's letters. Some suggest Mark (5:13) as the helper instead. John H. Elliott objects that the Greek of 5:12 names Silvanus as the letter's carrier, and that a secretary-author raises more problems than it solves. See the note at 5:12.

Many scholars, perhaps most today, see the letter as the work of Christians in Rome who carried on Peter's tradition after his death. Their reasons: the polished Greek and use of the Septuagint, unexpected from a Galilean fisherman; the closeness to Paul's letters (Romans, Ephesians); the name 'Babylon' for Rome, which Bart Ehrman and others date after AD 70; and a picture of suffering that some match with the time of Domitian or Trajan. Ehrman counts it as pseudonymous, and Graham Stanton rejected Petrine authorship, dating it to Domitian's reign. Against the last reason, Travis Williams argues that the suffering described need not be official Roman persecution, which leaves an earlier date open.

The Plain English Translation follows the text as written ('Peter'). The notes give each view where it matters. Whether written by Peter or in his name, the letter was accepted early and by all the churches.

audience.to: Christians scattered across Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, the Roman provinces of Asia Minor north of the Taurus Mountains, in cities, towns and villages. Many modern interpreters take them to be mainly Gentile converts: they had been ransomed from 'the futile way of life that your fathers passed on to you' (1:18) and had once done 'what the Gentiles want' (4:3). Others, from Eusebius to Calvin, have read the 'Dispersion' (1:1) as Jewish believers, or as mixed churches. Among them were household slaves with unbelieving masters (2:18), wives with unbelieving husbands (3:1), elders and younger members (5:1-5). They met in houses and depended on each other's hospitality (4:9).
audience.why: They were suffering, mostly through slander, insults and social pressure from neighbors and families who resented their new faith (2:12; 3:16; 4:4, 14), and they may have faced accusations 'as a Christian' (4:16). The letter gives them a new identity (chosen, born again, God's house and priesthood), a way to live under pressure (do good, submit where possible, answer gently, return blessing), and a hope that makes suffering bearable (the inheritance, the unveiling of Christ, the end of all things). Knowing that the readers were outsiders who had lost standing explains why the letter calls them 'resident aliens' and gives them Israel's titles: it turns their marginal place into a calling.
views: Eusebius, following Origen, says Peter 'preached in Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, Cappadocia, and Asia to the Jews of the dispersion' (Church History 3.1.2). Calvin held that 'dispersion' 'can apply only to the Jews' and that Peter, apostle to the circumcised (Galatians 2:7-8), 'designed this Epistle more especially for the Jews'.
Calvin's translator John Owen answered in a note that 'nothing decisive' shows it was 'written only to believing Jews', while 4:3 'seems clearly to shew that Peter included the believing Gentiles'.
Many modern interpreters, the NET Bible's notes among them, read 1:14, 1:18 and 4:3-4 as describing former pagans, and the 'Dispersion' as Israel's word applied to them.
John H. Elliott argued that many readers were resident aliens and strangers in a social and legal sense, and that the letter offers them a home in the household of God (as Moses Chin summarizes him).
Others, including Chin, hold that 'resident aliens' describes every believer's life on earth, as in Psalm 39:12 and Hebrews 11:13, whatever their legal status.

John H. Elliott and others read the suffering as local and social; others connect it with the trials Pliny describes in Bithynia-Pontus around AD 112, or with Domitian, though Paul Achtemeier finds no evidence of an official policy against Christians under Domitian.

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads 1 Peter against the Roman provinces of Asia Minor: converts, probably mostly Gentiles, who left their families' gods, house churches, slaves and wives in pagan households, provincial governors, the imperial cult, and the trials Pliny describes in Bithynia-Pontus.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the letter was made: Peter, Peter through Silvanus, or a Petrine circle in Rome; its date; its links with Paul's letters; possible hymns and creeds in 2:21-25 and 3:18-22; the purpose of the household code; and what the manuscripts read, including the changes made by the Editio Critica Maior.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Follows the letter's design: the frame of exile (Dispersion and Babylon), the chain of stone texts, the household code's pairs, the movement from suffering to glory, and its wordplays (trickery and no trickery, word and without a word).

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads the letter's use of Israel's Scriptures and titles (Exodus 19:6; Isaiah 40; 43; 53; Hosea 1-2; Psalm 34; Proverbs), the Dispersion, and the Watchers of 1 Enoch, and asks what it means that a church, probably mostly Gentile, is given Israel's names; it also notes how Jewish readers read the same texts.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: How the churches have read it: Peter in Rome, the priesthood of all believers, the descent into Hades in the creeds and the Easter icon, baptism that saves, church and state, and the long use of its household code.

sections.b:
1 Peter is short enough to read aloud in twenty minutes, as its first hearers did in their house churches. It moves in three steps. First, who you are: born again, chosen, God's house and priesthood (1:1-2:10). Second, how to live as outsiders: among neighbors, under the emperor, as slaves, wives and husbands, and toward slanderers (2:11-3:17). Third, why suffering does not have the last word: Christ suffered and now rules over every power; judgment begins at God's house; the God of all grace will restore you (3:18-5:14).

Key words are kept the same in the Plain English Translation so the reader can follow them: chosen (1:1; 2:4, 6, 9; 5:13), temporary residents and resident aliens (1:1, 17; 2:11), holy (1:15-16; 2:5, 9), do good (2:15, 20; 3:6, 17; 4:19), suffer, glory, grace, unveiled (1:7, 13; 4:13; 5:1) and trickery (2:1, 2, 22; 3:10).

Peter never mentions Israel, the Jews, the law or circumcision. Instead he gives his readers, probably mostly Gentiles, Israel's titles: chosen, the Dispersion, sprinkled with covenant blood, holy as God is holy, a royal priesthood and a holy nation, God's people (2:9-10, from Exodus 19:6, Isaiah 43:20-21 and Hosea). He calls their unbelieving neighbors 'the Gentiles' (2:12).

Christians have read this in different ways: that the church has replaced Israel as God's people; that Gentile believers have been joined to Israel's story without displacing Israel; or that Peter borrows Israel's language as a model for any people of God without saying anything about the Jewish people themselves. See the topic church-israel. Jewish readers note that these titles were given to Israel at Sinai for all its generations.

Unlike 2 Peter, 1 Peter was accepted early and widely. Polycarp of Smyrna echoes it many times early in the 100s. Eusebius, writing about AD 325, says 'One epistle of Peter, that called the first, is acknowledged as genuine', and lists it among the books all accepted, while 2 Peter was disputed (Church History 3.3.1; 3.25.2). It stands among the Catholic or General Letters, the seven letters (James to Jude) addressed to the church widely rather than to one congregation.

For the Catholic Letters (James to Jude), the Editio Critica Maior (ECM), the large critical edition made with the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method, is published, and the Nestle-Aland 28th edition took over its text, with changes in 34 places across these letters (as Peter Williams reports in his review of NA28). This site's base text is the SBL Greek New Testament, but in the Catholic Letters it follows NA28 where the two differ and the evidence allows. In 1 Peter that matters at 1:22 ('from a pure heart'), 4:16 ('in this matter', an ECM change), 5:1 ('To the elders', without 'so') and 5:11 ('forever'). Every difference that changes the English, including every place where the KJV reads differently, is shown in the variants.

The manuscript lists in the variants follow the NET Bible's text-critical notes. Numbers such as 01, 03 or 1739 and letters such as Ψ are the standard names of Greek manuscripts; P72 is a papyrus; 'P' (number 025) is Codex Porphyrianus, a ninth-century manuscript of Acts and the letters.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Noah's eight and the readers' few
spec.body: Peter stresses that in Noah's ark 'a few, eight souls, were carried safe' (3:20). I suggest he chose Noah over the Red Sea or the Jordan, the usual Old Testament pictures for baptism (compare 1 Corinthians 10:1-2), because Noah's family was a tiny minority surrounded by a disobedient world, which matched his readers' situation better than a whole nation passing through the sea. The theme of the righteous few also fits 4:18 ('if the righteous person is barely saved'). This overlaps with the common observation that the letter speaks to a small, slandered minority; the specific reason for choosing Noah is my suggestion.

prompts: A house church in a hill town of Asia Minor at dusk: men, women, slaves and children sit on mats while a reader holds up a papyrus letter. Above them, drawn like a cave painting in ochre, a great building is rising, each of its stones a small human figure, resting on one glowing cornerstone shaped like a man with wounded hands. Sketched on old parchment with charcoal and soft modern watercolor, torn edges, no hard rectangular frame.

A dark underground vault drawn in black ink and red ochre like an ancient cave painting, with chained winged figures crouching in shadow. Through a broken gate a single figure in white strides in, light spilling from him, holding up a scroll. In the top corner, tiny and far away, an ark floats on waves. Hand-sketched on a scroll in the style of an old manuscript, with modern brushwork, ragged edges.
The roaring lion and the shepherd

A shepherd with a staff stands between a small flock of sheep and a lion drawn in bold cave-painting strokes, its mouth open in a roar. The sheep are drawn as people huddled together. Above, written as if on a papyrus fragment, Greek letters fade into the sky. Sketched onto parchment with charcoal, ink washes and torn edges; soft, no sharp frame.
reading: John H. Elliott, 1 Peter, Anchor Bible 37B (2000)
A large commentary on the Greek by the scholar who made the social reading of 'resident aliens' central.
John H. Elliott, A Home for the Homeless: A Sociological Exegesis of 1 Peter (1981)
The study that read the readers as literal outsiders given a home in God's household.
William J. Dalton, Christ's Proclamation to the Spirits: A Study of 1 Peter 3:18-4:6, 2nd ed. (1989)
A book-length study of 1 Peter 3:18-4:6 and the spirits in prison.
